questions.question: What is the major reason for the shrinking of the Himalayan glaciers?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Global warming**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Global warming** is identified as the primary driver behind the rapid **shrinking and retreat** of **Himalayan glaciers**. This phenomenon refers to the long-term increase in the **average surface temperature** of the Earth due to human activities. ***Hence, the statement is correct.***
 
• The **Himalayas**, known as the **Third Pole**, hold the largest concentration of **frozen water** outside the North and South Poles. These glaciers are highly sensitive to **climatic fluctuations**.
 
• The primary mechanism of shrinking involves the **negative mass balance** of glaciers, where the rate of **ablation** (melting and evaporation) exceeds the rate of **accumulation** (snowfall) due to rising atmospheric temperatures.
 
• The accumulation of **Greenhouse Gases (GHGs)** such as **Carbon Dioxide (CO2)**, **Methane (CH4)**, and **Nitrous Oxide (N2O)** traps solar radiation within the Earth's atmosphere, creating a warming effect that accelerates the melting of **alpine glaciers**.
 
• According to various scientific assessments, the **Himalayan region** is warming at a rate higher than the **global average**, leading to the formation of **supraglacial lakes** and increased risks of **Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs)**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Black Carbon:** Apart from general global warming, the deposition of **Black Carbon** (soot) on glacier surfaces significantly contributes to melting. Produced by the **incomplete combustion** of fossil fuels and biomass, these dark particles reduce the **albedo effect** (reflectivity) of snow, causing it to absorb more **solar energy**.
 
• **ICIMOD Reports:** The **International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD)** released a landmark report stating that even if global warming is capped at **1.5 degrees Celsius**, at least **one-third** of the Himalayan glaciers will vanish by the year **2100**.
 
• **River Systems:** The shrinking of these glaciers directly impacts perennial river systems like the **Ganga**, **Indus**, and **Brahmaputra**. These rivers provide water security to nearly **1.9 billion people** across **India**, **China**, **Pakistan**, **Nepal**, and **Bhutan**.
 
• **The Gangotri Glacier:** Located in the **Uttarkashi district** of **Uttarakhand**, it is one of the largest glaciers in the Himalayas. It has been retreating at a rate of approximately **10 to 30 meters per year** over the last few decades.
 
• **Impact on Ecosystems:** The loss of glacial volume alters the **hydrological cycle**, leading to unpredictable **seasonal water flow**, which adversely affects **agriculture**, **hydroelectric power generation**, and **biodiversity** in the **Hindu Kush Himalayan (HKH)** region.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Paris Agreement (2015):** An international treaty aimed at limiting **global warming** to well below **2 degrees Celsius** above pre-industrial levels is crucial for the preservation of the **cryosphere**.
 
• **Satellite Monitoring:** Agencies like **ISRO** (Indian Space Research Organisation) and **NASA** use **Remote Sensing** and **GIS** technology to monitor the health of **over 9,000 glaciers** in the Indian Himalayan region.
 
• **Albedo Feedback:** As white ice melts, it exposes darker land or water underneath, which absorbs more heat, leading to a **self-reinforcing cycle** of further warming and melting.
 
• **Holocene Epoch:** While glaciers have advanced and retreated naturally over **geological time scales**, the current rate of retreat is unprecedented and primarily **anthropogenic** (human-induced).

questions.question: If a satellite is in the plane of the equator with 0 degrees inclination and at a height of about 36000 km then it is said to be in _______ orbit.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Geo-stationary**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• A geo-stationary orbit is a circular orbit located approximately 35,786 km (22,236 miles) above the equator.
 
• In this orbit, the satellite moves at the same rotational speed as Earth, making it appear stationary relative to an observer on Earth.
 
• This type of orbit is ideal for communication satellites, weather observation, and broadcasting purposes.
 
• Geo-stationary satellites have an inclination of 0 degrees, meaning they orbit in the Earth's equatorial plane.
 
• Examples of geo-stationary satellites include INSAT series satellites and weather monitoring systems like GOES.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Polar Orbit:**

 
 
• In a polar orbit, the satellite passes over the Earth's poles on each revolution.
 
• These orbits are typically used for Earth observation and remote sensing as they provide global coverage.
 
• Satellites in polar orbits have an inclination close to 90 degrees.
 
• An example of a polar orbit satellite is the NOAA series used for weather forecasting.
 
 
 
• **Elliptical Orbit:**
 
 
• Elliptical orbits are non-circular orbits where the satellite's distance from Earth varies throughout its revolution.
 
• These orbits are used for specific applications such as communication in high-latitude regions (e.g., Molniya orbits).
 
• The satellite spends more time near the apogee (farthest point from Earth), allowing extended coverage over a particular region.
 
 
 
• **Sun-Synchronous Orbit:**
 
 
• Sun-synchronous orbits are designed so that the satellite passes over the same part of the Earth at the same local solar time.
 
• This orbit ensures consistent lighting conditions, making it ideal for imaging and mapping purposes.
 
• These orbits are commonly used by Earth observation satellites like Landsat and Sentinel.

questions.question:
Which of the following statement is an example of contact force?

I. Electrostatic force

II. Friction
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only II**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Friction** is a type of **contact force**, as it arises when two surfaces are in direct contact and resist motion relative to each other. Thus, Statement II is **correct**.
 
• **Electrostatic force** is a type of **non-contact force**, as it acts between charged particles without requiring any physical contact. Hence, Statement I is **incorrect**.
 
• Contact forces are forces that occur when two objects are physically touching. Examples include frictional force, tension force, and normal force.
 
• Non-contact forces, like electrostatic, gravitational, and magnetic forces, act over a distance without direct physical interaction.
 
• In this question, only friction qualifies as a contact force, making the correct answer **Only II**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Contact forces:**

 
 
• **Friction:** A resistive force that opposes the motion of one surface relative to another. It can be static (prevents motion) or kinetic (opposes ongoing motion).
 
• **Normal force:** The support force exerted by a surface perpendicular to an object resting on it, e.g., a book on a table.
 
• **Tension:** A pulling force transmitted through a string, rope, or cable when it is pulled tight by forces acting at either end.
 
• **Applied force:** A force applied by a person or another object to move an object.
 
• **Air resistance:** A type of frictional force that acts against the motion of an object moving through the air.
 
 
 
• **Non-contact forces:**
 
 
• **Electrostatic force:** The force between charged particles, either attracting or repelling depending on their charges.
 
• **Gravitational force:** The attractive force between two masses, such as between the Earth and an object.
 
• **Magnetic force:** The attraction or repulsion between magnetic poles or between a magnet and a ferromagnetic material.
 
 
 
• **Key distinctions:** Contact forces require physical interaction between objects, while non-contact forces operate over a distance without physical touch.
 
• **Applications:** Friction is essential in daily life for activities like walking, driving, and holding objects, as it provides the necessary grip and resistance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Friction** can cause wear and tear on surfaces over time, but it is also crucial for enabling controlled motion.
 
• Electrostatic forces play a significant role in phenomena like lightning and the attraction of dust particles to surfaces.
 
• Understanding the difference between contact and non-contact forces is fundamental to studying mechanics and physics.
 
• In engineering, controlling friction is essential for optimizing machine performance and efficiency.

questions.question: A heating element of a heater is made of a material with high resistivity and high melting point. Which of the following material properties is most crucial for its function as a heating element?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**High resistivity**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **High resistivity** is crucial for a heating element as it ensures that a significant amount of electrical energy is converted into heat.
 
• Materials with high resistivity provide resistance to the flow of electric current, which causes the generation of heat due to Joule heating (*P = I²R*).
 
• Common materials used for heating elements, such as nichrome, have high resistivity and are efficient at producing heat.
 
• High resistivity reduces the risk of excessive current flow, thereby protecting the heating element and enhancing its longevity.
 
• Other properties like high melting point and corrosion resistance complement high resistivity to ensure the durability of the heating element.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Joule Heating:** The process by which electrical energy is converted into heat energy when current flows through a conductor with resistance.
 
• **High Melting Point:** Heating elements must withstand high temperatures without melting or deforming, ensuring safe and effective operation.
 
• **Thermal Conductivity:** While high thermal conductivity is beneficial for heat dissipation, heating elements typically focus on resistivity to generate heat efficiently.
 
• **Specific Heat Capacity:** Materials with low specific heat capacity heat up faster, but this property is secondary to resistivity in heating elements.
 
• **Nichrome:** An alloy commonly used for heating elements, composed of nickel and chromium, known for its high resistivity and corrosion resistance.

questions.question:
Read the statements carefully and choose the **correct **option:

**Assertion (A)**: Aluminium smelting is the most important metallurgical industry in India.

**Reason (R)**: Aluminium is used in the manufacture of aircraft, wires, and utensils.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**A is false, but R is true**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Assertion (A): Aluminium smelting is the most important metallurgical industry in India.** - This statement is **false** because while aluminium smelting is a significant industry, iron and steel production is considered the most important metallurgical industry in India due to its extensive applications in infrastructure, construction, transportation, and manufacturing.
 
• **Reason (R): Aluminium is used in the manufacture of aircraft, wires, and utensils.** - This statement is **true** as aluminium is widely utilized in various industries due to its lightweight, corrosion resistance, and high conductivity.
 
• Aluminium smelting involves extracting aluminium from bauxite ore through electrolysis, and India is one of the leading producers of aluminium.
 
• Aluminium's applications include its use in the aviation industry (aircraft bodies), electrical industry (wires and cables), and household utensils, making it a versatile material.
 
• Despite its importance, aluminium smelting ranks below iron and steel in terms of economic contribution and industrial significance in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Iron and Steel Industry:**
 
 
• It is regarded as the backbone of industrial development in India and is considered the most important metallurgical industry.
 
• Iron and steel are used extensively in construction, transportation, machinery manufacturing, and numerous other industries.
 
• India is one of the largest producers of crude steel globally, with major steel plants located in Bhilai, Rourkela, Durgapur, and Jamshedpur.
 
• The significance of iron and steel lies in their contribution to GDP, employment generation, and infrastructure development.
 
 
 
• **Aluminium Smelting:**
 
 
• India has abundant reserves of bauxite, the ore from which aluminium is extracted.
 
• Aluminium smelting is critical for producing lightweight materials used in the aerospace, automotive, and electrical industries.
 
• Major aluminium-producing companies in India include Hindalco Industries and the National Aluminium Company (NALCO).
 
 
 
• **Other Metallurgical Industries:**
 
 
• India also has significant copper smelting industries, which contribute to the electrical and electronic sectors.
 
• Lead and zinc are other metallurgical sectors that play crucial roles in batteries, galvanization, and industrial applications.
 
 
 
• **Bauxite and Aluminium:**
 
 
• Bauxite is the principal ore for aluminium, and India ranks among the top producers globally.
 
• Aluminium is highly valued for its lightweight, durability, and corrosion resistance, making it indispensable for modern industries.

questions.question: The first peptide to be produced after wounding in the tomato plant is _________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Systemin**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Systemin** is a small signaling peptide consisting of **18 amino acids** that mediates the systemic defense response in plants belonging to the **Solanaceae** family, particularly the **tomato** (Solanum lycopersicum).
 
• It was the first **polypeptide hormone** to be identified in plants, discovered in **1991** by **Clarence A. Ryan** and his research team.
 
• The peptide is synthesized from a larger precursor protein called **prosystemin**, which contains approximately **200 amino acids** and is located in the **cytosol** of vascular parenchyma cells.
 
• Upon **mechanical wounding** or **herbivore attack**, prosystemin is proteolytically cleaved by specific enzymes to release the active systemin peptide into the **apoplast** and **phloem**.
 
• Systemin travels through the **vascular system** to distal tissues, where it binds to a cell-surface receptor called **SR160** (a leucine-rich repeat receptor-like kinase).
 
• This binding initiates the **octadecanoid pathway**, leading to the rapid production of **Jasmonic Acid (JA)**, which subsequently induces the expression of **protease inhibitor** genes to deter pests.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Jasmonic acid (JA)**:

 
 
• A **lipid-derived** phytohormone synthesized from **linolenic acid**.
 
• While central to wound signaling, it is a **cyclopentanone** derivative and not a peptide.
 
 
 
• **Salicylic acid (SA)**:
 
 
• A **phenolic** hormone primarily involved in defense against **biotrophic pathogens**.
 
• It plays a key role in **Systemic Acquired Resistance (SAR)**, often acting antagonistically to the jasmonic acid pathway.
 
 
 
• **Ricin**:
 
 
• A highly toxic **Type II ribosome-inactivating protein (RIP)** extracted from **castor beans** (Ricinus communis).
 
• It functions as a **cytotoxin** rather than a signaling peptide for wound response in tomato plants.

questions.question: Why do single-celled organisms do not need specific organs for taking in food, exchanging gases, or removing wastes?

options.text: Their entire surface is in contact with the environment
They have a protective wall around them
They do not perform these functions

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Their entire surface is in contact with the environment**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Single-celled organisms**, such as amoeba, paramecium, or bacteria, are microscopic organisms that consist of only one cell. Their **entire surface is in direct contact with the environment**, allowing them to carry out all essential life processes without specialized organs.
 
• Their small size and large surface-area-to-volume ratio enable them to exchange substances like **oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients, and waste products** efficiently through simple diffusion. **This is why they do not need specialized respiratory or excretory organs.**
 
• These organisms absorb nutrients from their surroundings through mechanisms like **endocytosis**, wherein the cell membrane engulfs food particles.
 
• Waste products are also expelled directly into the external environment via simple processes like exocy

questions.question: Why is hydrogen used as fuel in a cryogenic engine?

options.text: Because it is easy to store at room temperature.
Because it has the highest energy output per kilogram.
Because it is very cheap in comparison to other fuels.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Because it has the highest energy output per kilogram**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Hydrogen** is widely used as a fuel in cryogenic engines because it has the **highest energy output per kilogram**. This makes it an extremely efficient fuel source, especially for applications like space exploration where energy density is crucial.
 
• With a **specific energy of approximately 142 MJ/kg**, hydrogen far exceeds the energy output of conventional fuels like gasoline or kerosene.
 
• In cryogenic engines, hydrogen is used in its liquid form (**liquid hydrogen or LH2**), which requires extremely low temperatures (**-253°C**) to remain in a liquid state. This enhances its energy density and usability in such applications.
 
• Other properties of hydrogen, such as its **low molecular weight** and ability to produce only water as a by-product when burned with oxygen, make it an environmentally friendly and efficient option for cryogenic engines.
 
• The use of hydrogen as a fuel is particularly significant in the **aerospace industry**, where it powers rockets like the Space Shuttle Main

questions.question: What is the audible frequency range for the human ear?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**20-20,000 Hz**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• The **audible frequency range for the human ear** typically spans from **20 Hz to 20,000 Hz**. This range is considered the standard for human hearing across different age groups and conditions.

• Frequencies below **20 Hz** are referred to as **infrasound**, and frequencies above **20,000 Hz** are called **ultrasound**. These are outside the range of human hearing.

• The sensitivity of human hearing varies with frequency. Humans are most sensitive to sounds in the range of approximately **2 kHz to 5 kHz**, which corresponds to everyday sounds like speech.

• As humans age, the ability to hear higher frequencies diminishes. For instance, older individuals may lose sensitivity to sounds above **15,000 Hz**.

• The audible range is crucial for various applications such as **speech communication, music, and acoustic engineering**, ensuring devices like headphones and speakers cater to this range.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Characteristics of Human Hearing:** 

• Humans can perceive both **pitch (frequency)** and **intensity (loudness)** of sound waves within the audible range.

• The **threshold of hearing** (minimum audible sound) is around **0 dB**, while the threshold of pain is approximately **120-130 dB**.

• Hearing ability is influenced by factors such as **age, environment, and health conditions**.

• **Infrasound:** 

• Frequencies below **20 Hz** are known as infrasound. These are produced by natural phenomena like **earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and ocean waves**.

• Though humans cannot hear infrasound, it can be felt as vibrations and has applications in **seismic monitoring**.

• **Ultrasound:** 

• Frequencies above **20,000 Hz** are termed ultrasound. It is widely used in **medical imaging, industrial applications, and cleaning**.

• Animals such as **bats and dolphins** can hear ultrasound and utilize it for navigation and communication.

• **Applications of Audible Range Knowledge:** 

• Design of audio equipment like **microphones, speakers, and headphones** is based on the human audible range.

• Technological advancements in fields like **telecommunications, music production, and hearing aids** rely on understanding the auditory spectrum.

• **Important Facts:** 

• The **human auditory system** includes the outer ear, middle ear, and inner ear, working together to process sound waves.

• The study of human hearing is essential in disciplines such as **audiology, acoustics, and psychoacoustics**.

• Hearing tests, such as **pure tone audiometry**, are used to determine the audible frequency range of individuals.

questions.question: How have human-induced disturbances impacted terrestrial ecosystems?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Through changes in land use**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Human-induced disturbances** have significantly impacted **terrestrial ecosystems** primarily through **land use changes**, which include activities such as **deforestation**, **urbanization**, and the conversion of natural landscapes into **agricultural land**.
 
• **Deforestation** for timber or farming leads to the immediate loss of **habitats**, reduction in **biodiversity**, and disruption of the **carbon cycle**.
 
• **Urbanization** results in **habitat fragmentation**, where large, continuous ecosystems are broken into smaller, isolated patches, making it difficult for species to survive and migrate.
 
• **Agricultural expansion** often involves the use of **monocultures**, which reduces the resilience of the ecosystem and alters **soil health** and **nutrient cycling**.
 
• While **rising ocean temperatures** (Option 3) are a result of human activity, they primarily impact **marine ecosystems** rather than being a direct terrestrial disturbance.
 
• **Atmospheric CO2 concentrations** (Option 4) have actually **increased** due to human activities like burning **fossil fuels**, rather than decreased.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• According to the **Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)**, approximately 75% of the Earth's ice-free land surface has been significantly altered by **human actions**.
 
• **Anthropogenic disturbances** also include the introduction of **invasive species**, **pollution** (pesticides and heavy metals), and **overexploitation** of natural resources.
 
• **Land degradation** caused by human activity affects the livelihoods of billions of people and contributes to **climate change** by releasing stored carbon from vegetation and soils.
 
• The **United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 15** specifically aims to protect, restore, and promote the sustainable use of **terrestrial ecosystems** and halt **biodiversity loss**.

questions.question:
Read the below statements about enzymes and choose the correct option:

1. Enzymes increase the activation energy of a reaction.

2. Enzymes are specific to substrates due to active site configuration.

3. Enzyme activity is affected by pH and temperature. Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 2**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Statement 2:** Enzymes are specific to substrates due to active site configuration, is correct because enzymes have a unique three-dimensional structure that allows them to bind specifically to their corresponding substrates.
 
• **Statement 3:** Enzyme activity is affected by pH and temperature, is correct because enzymes work optimally within specific pH and temperature ranges, and deviations can lead to denaturation or reduced activity.
 
• Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up biochemical reactions by lowering the activation energy required for the reaction to occur.
 
• Specificity of enzymes is governed by the "lock and key" model or "induced fit" model, where the substrate fits perfectly into the enzyme's active site.
 
• pH affects the ionization of enzyme active sites, while temperature influences the kinetic energy of molecules, impacting enzyme efficiency.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Statement 1:** Enzymes increase the activation energy of a reaction, is incorrect because enzymes lower the activation energy, enabling reactions to occur more efficiently and faster.
 
• **Activation Energy:** This is the minimum energy required for reactants to form products in a chemical reaction. Enzymes reduce this energy barrier by stabilizing the transition state.
 
• **Denaturation:** Extreme changes in pH or temperature can denature enzymes, altering their structure and rendering them inactive.
 
• **Enzyme Specificity:** The specificity of enzymes is crucial for metabolic pathways, preventing unwanted reactions and maintaining cellular function.
 
• **Main Theme:** The question focuses on understanding the fundamental properties of enzymes, their specificity, and how external factors like pH and temperature impact their activity.

questions.question:
Which of the following organ is part of excretory system in human human body? 

I. A pair of ureters

II. A urethra
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both I and II**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The human excretory system** is responsible for the elimination of metabolic waste products and toxins from the body, ensuring homeostasis.
 
• **Statement I: A pair of ureters** – Ureters are part of the excretory system. They are two tubes that transport urine from the kidneys to the urinary bladder. *Hence, this statement is correct.*
 
• **Statement II: A urethra** – The urethra is also part of the excretory system. It is a tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body during urination. *Hence, this statement is correct.*
 
• Both **ureters** and the **urethra** play key roles in the proper functioning of the urinary system, which is a crucial component of the excretory system.
 
• As both statements are correct, the correct answer is **Both I and II**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Components of the human excretory system:**

 
 
• The system consists of the **kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, and urethra**.
 
• The **kidneys** filter blood to remove waste products and excess substances, forming urine.
 
• The **ureters** are muscular tubes that transport urine from the kidneys to the urinary bladder.
 
• The **urinary bladder** stores urine temporarily until it is expelled from the body.
 
• The **urethra** is the final part of the system that allows urine to exit the body.
 
 
 
• **Functions of the excretory system:**
 
 
• Regulation of water and electrolyte balance in the body.
 
• Removal of metabolic waste products like urea, uric acid, and creatinine.
 
• Detoxification of harmful substances.
 
• Maintaining blood pressure and pH levels.
 
 
 
• **Diseases related to the excretory system:**
 
 
• **Kidney stones:** Hard deposits of minerals and salts that can obstruct the urinary flow.
 
• **Urinary tract infections (UTIs):** Infections in the urinary system caused by bacteria.
 
• **Chronic kidney disease:** Gradual loss of kidney function over time.
 
 
 
• **Importance of hydration:** Drinking sufficient water aids in the efficient functioning of the excretory system and prevents conditions like kidney stones and UTIs.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Role of the ureters:** Ureters are approximately 25–30 cm long and use peristaltic movements to transport urine from the kidneys to the bladder.
 
• **Role of the urethra:** The length of the urethra varies between males and females. In males, it also serves as a passage for semen during reproduction.
 
• **Excretion vs. Egestion:** Excretion refers to the removal of metabolic waste, whereas egestion involves the elimination of undigested food residue from the digestive system.
 
• **Clinical relevance:** Diagnostic tools like urinalysis and imaging techniques (e.g., ultrasounds) are used to assess the health of the excretory system.

questions.question: Tracheid is part of which plant tissue?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Xylem**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Tracheids** are elongated, tube-like cells with thick, **lignified walls** and tapering ends that serve as the primary conducting elements of the **Xylem**.
 
• They are **dead cells** at maturity, meaning they lack **protoplasm**, which allows them to function efficiently as hollow tubes for water transport. ***Hence, option 1 is correct.***
 
• The main function of tracheids is the **conduction of water and minerals** from the roots to various parts of the plant, such as the stem and leaves.
 
• In **Pteridophytes** and **Gymnosperms**, tracheids are the only water-conducting elements, whereas **Angiosperms** (flowering plants) possess both tracheids and **vessels**.
 
• Apart from conduction, the thick, lignified walls of tracheids provide significant **mechanical support** to the plant body, helping it stand upright.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Xylem (Complex Permanent Tissue):**

 
 
• The term **Xylem** was introduced by **Carl Nägeli** in **1858**.
 
• It is composed of four distinct types of elements: **Tracheids**, **Vessels**, **Xylem Parenchyma**, and **Xylem Fibers**.
 
• **Xylem Parenchyma** is the only **living component** of the xylem and is responsible for storing food materials like starch and fats.
 
• **Vessels** are long cylindrical structures with perforated end walls, forming continuous channels for water flow, a characteristic feature of **Angiosperms**.
 
 
 
• **Phloem:**
 
 
• **Phloem** is responsible for the **translocation of organic food** (sucrose) from the leaves (source) to other parts of the plant (sink). ***Hence, option 2 is incorrect.***
 
• It consists of **Sieve tubes**, **Companion cells**, **Phloem parenchyma**, and **Phloem fibers**.
 
• Unlike xylem, phloem transport is **bidirectional**, allowing nutrients to move both up and down the plant.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Cuticle:**

 
 
• The **Cuticle** is a protective, waxy, and water-repellent layer covering the **epidermis** of leaves, young shoots, and other aerial plant organs. ***Hence, option 3 is incorrect.***
 
• Its primary function is to **minimize water loss** through transpiration and protect the plant against **pathogens** and mechanical injury.
 
 
 
• **Bark:**
 
 
• **Bark** is a non-technical term used to describe all tissues **outside the vascular cambium**, including the secondary phloem, periderm, and phellogen. ***Hence, option 4 is incorrect.***
 
• It forms during **secondary growth** in woody plants and acts as a protective outer covering against **environmental stress** and physical damage.
 
 
 
• **Structural Differences:**
 
 
• **Tracheids** possess **pits** (thin areas in the cell wall) through which water passes from cell to cell, whereas **vessels** have **perforation plates** at their ends for more rapid conduction.
 
• The presence of **Lignin** in tracheid walls is a crucial evolutionary adaptation that allowed plants to grow tall by providing **structural rigidity**.

questions.question: The object covers unequal distances in equal intervals of time, it is said to be in ____ motion.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**non-uniform motion**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In **non-uniform motion**, an object covers **unequal distances** in **equal intervals** of time. This is the defining characteristic of non-uniform motion.
 
• **Non-uniform motion** occurs when the speed of an object is not constant and changes as it moves. This can include acceleration or deceleration.
 
• Examples of **non-uniform motion** include a car speeding up or slowing down, a falling object under gravity, or a ball rolling down a hill.
 
• Graphically, the motion is represented by a **non-linear path** or a curved line when plotting distance versus time.
 
• The motion can be influenced by external factors like **force, friction, or gravity**, which cause changes in speed or direction.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Characteristics of Motion:**

 
 
• **Uniform motion:** An object covers equal distances in equal intervals of time. Examples include a car moving at a constant speed or the Earth revolving around the Sun.
 
• **Non-uniform motion:** The speed of the object changes, resulting in unequal distances covered in equal intervals of time. It can include both accelerated and decelerated motion.
 
 
 
• **Factors affecting non-uniform motion:**
 
 
• **Force:** A net external force can cause a change in the velocity, leading to non-uniform motion.
 
• **Gravity:** Objects falling under gravity exhibit non-uniform motion as their speed increases due to acceleration.
 
• **Friction:** Friction can slow down an object, causing non-uniform motion.
 
 
 
• **Examples of non-uniform motion:**
 
 
• A car accelerating on a highway or decelerating at a traffic signal.
 
• A roller coaster moving along a track with varying speeds and directions.
 
• A ball dropped from a height, which gains speed due to gravity.
 
 
 
• **Graphical representation:**
 
 
• In non-uniform motion, the **distance-time graph** is typically a curved line, indicating changes in speed over time.
 
• In contrast, the **velocity-time graph** may show variable slopes depending on acceleration or deceleration.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Newton’s Laws of Motion:**

 
 
• **First Law:** An object remains in uniform motion or at rest unless acted upon by an external force.
 
• **Second Law:** The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass.
 
• **Third Law:** For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.
 
 
 
• **Real-life applications:**
 
 
• Understanding non-uniform motion is critical in designing vehicles, braking systems, and amusement park rides.
 
• It is essential in calculating trajectories of projectiles and space missions.

questions.question: What causes water droplets to form on the outer surface of a glass containing ice-cold water?

options.text: Water vapour in the air condenses upon contact with the cold glass.
The glass is absorbing moisture from the air.
The glass is heating up the surrounding air.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Water vapour in the air condenses upon contact with the cold glass**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The atmosphere contains water in a gaseous state known as **water vapour**, which is invisible to the naked eye.
 
• When air moves near a glass containing ice-cold water, the **temperature gradient** causes heat to transfer from the warmer air to the colder surface of the glass.
 
• As the water vapour molecules lose **kinetic energy** due to this cooling effect, they slow down and begin to cluster together.
 
• This physical change from a gaseous phase to a liquid phase is called **condensation**.
 
• The **dew point** is the specific temperature at which the air becomes saturated and cannot hold all its water vapour, leading to the formation of the liquid **droplets** seen on the exterior surface.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Phase Transitions**:

 
 
• **Condensation**: An **exothermic process** where gas releases heat to become a liquid. It is the fundamental reason behind cloud formation and morning dew.
 
• **Evaporation**: The reverse process where liquid turns into gas. It is an **endothermic process** that requires heat absorption from the surroundings.
 
 
 
• **Properties of Glass**:
 
 
• Glass is an **impermeable** and **non-porous** material, meaning water cannot leak through the solid walls of the container.
 
• The appearance of water on the outside is entirely due to **atmospheric moisture** rather than the liquid inside the glass.
 
 
 
• **Humidity Factors**:
 
 
• The rate of droplet formation depends on **relative humidity**; higher humidity levels mean there is more water vapour available to condense, making the effect more pronounced.

questions.question: A sound wave has a frequency of 5 { kHz} and wave length 50 { cm} . How long (in seconds) will it take to travel 5 { km} ?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• To find the time taken by the sound wave to travel a certain distance, we first need to determine the **speed of the sound wave** using the given **frequency** and **wavelength**.
 
• The **frequency (f)** of the sound wave is given as **5 kHz**. Converting this to the standard SI unit, **1 kHz = 1000 Hz**, thus the frequency is **5000 Hz**.
 
• The **wavelength (λ)** is given as **50 cm**. Converting this to meters (SI unit), **100 cm = 1 m**, so the wavelength is **0.5 m**.
 
• The **speed (v)** of a wave is calculated using the formula: **v = f × λ**. By substituting the values: **v = 5000 Hz × 0.5 m = 2500 m/s**.
 
• The **distance (d)** to be traveled is **5 km**. Converting this to meters, **1 km = 1000 m**, so the distance is **5000 m**.
 
• The **time (t)** taken is calculated using the formula: **t = distance / speed**. Substituting the values: **t = 5000 m / 2500 m/s = 2 seconds**. ***Hence, the time taken is 2 seconds.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Frequency:** It refers to the number of complete oscillations or cycles a wave makes per unit of time. The **SI unit** of frequency is the **Hertz (Hz)**, named after **Heinrich Hertz**. In this problem, the **high frequency** of **5000 Hz** indicates an ultrasonic or high-pitched sound.
 
• **Wavelength:** This is the **minimum distance** after which the sound wave repeats itself, typically measured between two consecutive **crests** or **compressions**. Its **SI unit** is the **meter (m)**.
 
• **Wave Speed:** The speed of sound depends on the **medium** through which it travels. In this calculation, the speed was found to be **2500 m/s**, which is significantly higher than the speed of sound in **air** (approximately **343 m/s** at **20°C**). This suggests the wave is likely traveling through a **solid** or a dense **liquid**, as sound travels fastest in **solids**.
 
• **Distance and Time:** The linear relationship between **distance**, **speed**, and **time** assumes that the wave speed remains **constant** throughout the journey. In real-world scenarios, factors like **temperature** and **humidity** can alter the speed of sound over a **5 km** stretch.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Unit Conversions:** It is crucial to convert all units to the **International System of Units (SI)** before performing calculations.

 
 
• **1 kilometer (km) = 1000 meters (m)**.
 
• **1 kilohertz (kHz) = 1000 hertz (Hz)**.
 
• **1 centimeter (cm) = 0.01 meters (m)**.
 
 
 
• **The Wave Equation:** The fundamental relation **v = fλ** applies to all types of waves, including **longitudinal sound waves** and **transverse light waves**.
 
• **Audible Range:** Human ears can typically hear sounds with frequencies between **20 Hz and 20,000 Hz (20 kHz)**. Since the frequency in the question is **5 kHz**, it falls well within the **audible range** for humans.

questions.question: Which of the following species of big cat cannot roar?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Cheetah**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Cheetahs**, unlike other big cats such as tigers, leopards, and jaguars, **cannot roar**. Instead, they communicate with chirps, growls, purrs, and other vocalizations.
 
• The inability of cheetahs to roar is due to the anatomy of their voice box. They have a fixed structure in their larynx, which allows them to purr but not produce the deep, resonating roar typical of other big cats.
 
• The roaring ability in big cats is attributed to the presence of an elastic ligament in their hyoid bone, which cheetahs lack. This ligament is essential for producing the low-frequency sound of a roar.
 
• Leopards, tigers, and jaguars all belong to the genus **Panthera**, which is characterized by the ability to roar. Cheetahs, on the other hand, belong to the genus **Acinonyx**, which does not include roaring species.
 
• The cheetah's unique vocalizations, such as chirping, help them communicate with their cubs and other cheetahs in the wild, especially over short distances.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Leopard:**

 
 
• Leopards belong to the genus **Panthera** and are capable of roaring.
 
• They are found in sub-Saharan Africa, parts of Asia, and the Indian subcontinent.
 
• Their roars are used for territorial marking and to warn off rivals or predators.
 
 
 
• **Tiger:**
 
 
• Tigers, also part of the genus **Panthera**, are known for their loud and powerful roars.
 
• They use their roar for communication, territorial marking, and mating calls.
 
• Tigers are mostly found in dense forests in Asia, including India, Siberia, and Southeast Asia.
 
 
 
• **Jaguar:**
 
 
• Jaguars are native to Central and South America and are part of the genus **Panthera**.
 
• They are capable of roaring, which helps them establish dominance and communicate with others.
 
• Jaguars are often found in tropical rainforests and other dense habitats.
 
 
 
• **Cheetah:**
 
 
• Cheetahs are classified under the genus **Acinonyx**, distinguishing them from roaring big cats.
 
• They are known for their extraordinary speed, capable of reaching up to **70 mph (112 km/h)** in short bursts.
 
• Cheetahs are typically found in savannas and grasslands of Africa and parts of Iran.
 
• Their social structure is different, with males often forming coalitions, while females are solitary or stay with their cubs.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The ability to roar in big cats is determined by the structure of their hyoid bone and the presence of an elastic ligament.
 
• Cheetahs, being the fastest land animals, rely more on speed and agility for hunting rather than roaring for territorial dominance or communication.
 
• The differences in vocal abilities among big cats highlight the diversity in their evolutionary adaptations, which are shaped by their respective habitats and lifestyles.
 
• Conservation efforts are crucial for all big cat species, as many face threats from habitat loss, poaching, and human-wildlife conflict.

questions.question: Which of the following part of brain is responsible for the precision of voluntary actions and maintaining the posture and balance of the body?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Cerebellum**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• The **Cerebellum** is a part of the hindbrain that plays a critical role in coordinating **voluntary actions**, ensuring precision and smoothness of movements. 
• It is responsible for maintaining the body's **posture and balance**, allowing individuals to perform tasks such as walking, running, or standing upright. 
• The cerebellum processes sensory inputs from muscles, joints, and inner ear structures (vestibular system) to ensure proper motor control and coordination. 
• It also helps in fine-tuning motor activities like writing, typing, or playing musical instruments by regulating muscle movements. 
• Damage to the cerebellum can result in motor disorders such as **ataxia**, characterized by uncoordinated movements and difficulty maintaining balance. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Cerebrum:** 
• The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain and is associated with higher cognitive functions such as **thinking, memory, reasoning, and problem-solving**. 
• It is divided into two hemispheres, each responsible for controlling the opposite side of the body. 
• It also governs sensory perception and voluntary muscle movements but does not specialize in precision or balance. 
• **Medulla:** 
• The medulla, part of the brainstem, is primarily responsible for controlling **involuntary functions** such as breathing, heart rate, and blood pressure. 
• While vital for survival, it does not play a direct role in coordinating voluntary movements or maintaining body balance. 
• **Hypothalamus:** 
• The hypothalamus is a small but crucial part of the brain that regulates **homeostasis**, including body temperature, hunger, thirst, and hormonal balance. 
• It is involved in emotional responses and the endocrine system but does not contribute to motor coordination or posture. 
• **Function of Cerebellum:** 
• The cerebellum integrates sensory information from the **vestibular apparatus** (inner ear), visual signals, and proprioceptors (muscle/joint sensors). 
• It ensures smooth and accurate execution of motor activities, critical for tasks requiring precision, such as sports, dance, or surgical procedures. 
• It is located at the back of the brain, below the cerebrum, and connects with the spinal cord and other brain structures. 
• Modern research indicates its role in cognitive functions like attention and language in addition to motor skills. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Evolutionary Perspective:** The cerebellum is evolutionarily ancient and is present in most vertebrates, highlighting its importance in motor control. 
• **Clinical Application:** Damage to the cerebellum is assessed through tests like finger-to-nose coordination and heel-to-shin tests in neurological evaluations. 
• **Neuroplasticity:** The cerebellum exhibits neuroplasticity, meaning it can adapt and reorganize functions after injury, emphasizing its dynamic role in motor learning. </ul

questions.question: The amount of heat energy that is required to change 1 kg of a solid into liquid at atmospheric pressure at its melting point is known as the ____ heat of fusion.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**latent heat of fusion**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Latent heat of fusion** is the amount of heat energy required to change **1 kg of a solid into liquid** at its **melting point** under atmospheric pressure without any change in temperature.
 
• The energy supplied is used to overcome the **forces of attraction between particles** in the solid, allowing it to transition into a liquid state.
 
• This concept is important in understanding phase transitions in substances, such as when **ice melts to water** or metals are melted for industrial applications.
 
• The latent heat of fusion is specific to each substance and is usually measured in **joules per kilogram (J/kg)**.
 
• For example, the latent heat of fusion of **water** is approximately **334,000 J/kg**, meaning it takes this much energy to convert 1 kg of ice at 0°C to water at 0°C.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Phase Transitions:**

 
 
• When a substance transitions between solid, liquid, and gas phases, energy is absorbed or released without changing its temperature.
 
• **Latent heat of vaporization:** The energy required to convert a liquid into a gas without a temperature change.
 
• **Sublimation:** The direct conversion of a solid into a gas, bypassing the liquid phase. This process also involves latent heat.
 
 
 
• **Boiling Point vs. Melting Point:**
 
 
• The **boiling point** is the temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas, while the **melting point** is the temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid.
 
• Both processes require energy input, but the type of latent heat involved differs: fusion for melting, vaporization for boiling.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Latent Heat:**
 
 
• Used in **refrigeration and air conditioning systems** to absorb and release heat efficiently.
 
• Plays a critical role in **meteorological phenomena**, such as the formation of clouds and precipitation.
 
• Important in industrial processes like **metal casting** and **welding**, where substances are melted and reshaped.
 
 
 
• **Specific Characteristics of Related Options:**
 
 
• **Boiling:** Refers to the phase transition from liquid to gas, requiring latent heat of vaporization.
 
• **Melting:** Refers to the physical transition from solid to liquid, governed by latent heat of fusion.
 
• **Absolute:** This term is unrelated to phase transitions; it typically refers to numerical values such as absolute temperature.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Measurement Units:** Latent heat is commonly measured in **Joules (J)**, and its value depends on the substance's physical properties and phase transition.
 
• **Example Values:** The latent heat of fusion for ice is **334,000 J/kg**, while the latent heat of vaporization for water is approximately **2,260,000 J/kg**.
 
• **Scientific Significance:** Understanding latent heat is fundamental to thermodynamics, phase equilibria, and material science.
 
• **Practical Use:** This concept is utilized in designing systems like **heat exchangers**, **thermal storage devices**, and **cryogenic cooling systems**.

questions.question: Which of the following planet appears blue from the outer space because of its two-thirds surface is covered by water?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Earth**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Earth** is famously known as the **Blue Planet** because approximately **71%** (roughly **two-thirds**) of its surface is covered by **water**.
 
• When viewed from **outer space**, the vast **oceans** reflect **sunlight** and scatter blue light, giving the planet its distinctive and vibrant **blue appearance**.
 
• It is the **third planet** from the **Sun** and is the only known celestial body in the universe to support **life**, primarily due to the presence of **liquid water**.
 
• The **Earth's atmosphere**, composed of **78% Nitrogen** and **21% Oxygen**, also contributes to this appearance through a phenomenon called **Rayleigh scattering**, which makes the sky look blue from the surface and enhances the blue tint from space.
 
• The planet possesses a **magnetic field** generated by its **molten iron core**, which protects the **hydrosphere** and **atmosphere** from **solar winds**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mercury**:

 
 
• It is the **smallest planet** in the **Solar System** and the **closest** to the **Sun**.
 
• **Mercury** has almost no **atmosphere** to retain heat, leading to extreme **surface temperatures** ranging from **-173°C** at night to **427°C** during the day.
 
• Its surface is heavily **cratered** and appears **grey** or **dark brown**, similar to the **Moon**.
 
 
 
• **Venus**:
 
 
• Commonly referred to as **Earth's sister planet** or **twin** because of its similar **size** and **mass**.
 
• It is the **hottest planet** in the solar system due to a thick **atmosphere** primarily composed of **Carbon Dioxide**, which traps heat via a runaway **greenhouse effect**.
 
• **Venus** appears **bright yellowish-white** from space because of its thick clouds of **sulfuric acid**.
 
 
 
• **Uranus**:
 
 
• Classified as an **Ice Giant**, it is the **seventh planet** from the **Sun**.
 
• It appears **pale blue or cyan**, but this is not due to liquid water; rather, the **Methane** in its **atmosphere** absorbs **red light** and reflects **blue-green light**.
 
• It has a unique **tilt** of about **98 degrees**, meaning it effectively **rotates on its side**.
 
 
 
• **Mars**:
 
 
• Known as the **Red Planet**, its color is caused by the prevalence of **Iron Oxide** (rust) on its surface.
 
• It contains **Olympus Mons**, the **highest mountain** and **volcano** discovered in the **Solar System**.

• **The Solar System** consists of **eight planets**, divided into **Terrestrial planets** (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) and **Jovian planets** or Gas Giants (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune).
 
• **Earth** is the **densest planet** in the **Solar System** and the **largest** of the **terrestrial planets**.
 
• The **Earth** completes one **rotation** on its **axis** in **23 hours, 56 minutes, and 4 seconds**, and one **revolution** around the **Sun** in **365.25 days**.
 
• The distance between the **Earth** and the **Sun** is approximately **150 million kilometers**, a distance defined as one **Astronomical Unit (AU)**.
